outcome: Since 26 January 2024 one event bears on the core question of this entry, the discrete symmetric rendezvous problem (Mozart Café / Anderson–Weber): Cembrano, Fischer and Klimm (arXiv:2604.02058, first posted 2 April 2026, v2 2 August 2026) show the Anderson–Weber strategy is not optimal for any n ≥ 4, leaving the optimal value for n ≥ 4 and the asymptotic constant (about 0.829n) open; the other in-window events concern variants (a sphere/astronaut talk in February 2024, a deterministic labelled-line result in May 2025, and a restricted-strategy line model in September 2026) and do not settle the discrete problem.
problem_asks: The bullet is the bare title 'Rendezvous problem' under Games and puzzles > Games with imperfect information. The statement itself asks for nothing explicit, so the parts below come from the article it links to ('Rendezvous problem', the rendezvous search family) and from Richard Weber's list of unsolved problems (which calls its discrete symmetric question 'The Rendezvous Problem'). The parts are: (A) the symmetric rendezvous problem on n discrete locations (called the Mozart Café problem in the literature): for each n, the minimal expected time until two players who must use the same randomised strategy land on the same location. (A1) Whether the Anderson–Weber strategy is optimal for each n (settled for n = 2 and n = 3; open for n ≥ 4 until arXiv:2604.02058). (A2) The asymptotic constant c in expected time about c·n: Anderson–Weber gives about 0.829n, and the optimal c is not known. (A3) Anderson and Weber's question whether the optimal expected time increases with n. (B) Continuous rendezvous: symmetric and asymmetric versions on the line, the plane and the sphere (the astronaut problem), with known or unknown initial distance, including the symmetric value on the line at initial distance 2. (C) Deterministic (labelled-agent) rendezvous, which the article treats in a section of its own. The statement does not say which of (A) to (C) is meant. Part (A) is the one the article and Weber describe as open; (B) and (C) are variant families whose events are recorded below and labelled where they are different questions.

events.what_happened: E. J. Anderson and R. R. Weber, 'The rendezvous problem on discrete locations', J. Appl. Prob. 1990. Introduces the symmetric discrete problem with n locations and the Anderson–Weber strategy (stay at a home location with probability p, otherwise tour the other n−1 locations in random order, in blocks of n−1 steps), giving expected time below 0.829n for large n. States that for n = 2 the optimal strategy (p = 1/2, expected time 2) is established and claims the same for n = 3 (expected time 8/3). Discusses open questions for general n but does not characterise the optimum.
events.delivers: For n = 2, the optimal symmetric strategy and its value 2 are established. For n = 3 the paper claims the optimal strategy and value 8/3, but that claim is wrong (see disputes). For general n it gives an upper bound of about 0.829n on the optimal expected time, not an optimum.
events.remains: For n ≥ 3 the optimum is not established by this paper (the n = 3 claim is in error). For all n the optimal value, its asymptotic constant and the monotonicity question are open.

checked_by.who: Journal of Applied Probability (refereed journal; referees not named in the sources I read)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the result
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper; the n = 3 claim it contains was later found to be wrong, so refereeing did not catch that error

events.time_since_posted: 34 years at the frozen revision (36 years as of today)
events.directly_checkable: The n = 2 case (choose a uniformly random location each step, expected time 2) can be checked by hand.
events.doubts: The paper's n = 3 optimality claim was wrong. Its own discussion section (as summarised on Weber's abstract page) says the n = 3 claim contained an error, and a valid proof came about 15 years later. Cembrano, Fischer and Klimm (2026) say the same, but none of the sources I read describes the specific error.
events.direction: Partly confirms (n = 2, which is optimal) and partly wrong (the n = 3 claim). For general n it is an upper bound and an open question, not a resolution.
events.object: The Anderson–Weber strategy: a symmetric randomised strategy in blocks of n−1 steps, with home-stay probability p. It is explicit and constructive; for large n it gives expected time below 0.829n.

events.what_happened: Alpern and Gal (1995), asymmetric rendezvous on the line with known initial distance D: the least expected meeting time is 13D/8, achieved by a modification of 'wait for Mommy' in which the second player makes a short excursion. Cited by later papers (Alpern and Beck 1999; Leone and Alpern, arXiv:1611.05205). I did not open the original.
events.delivers: For the asymmetric continuous line with known initial distance D, the optimal expected meeting time 13D/8. This is the asymmetric (distinct roles) case, not the symmetric one.
events.remains: Does not address the symmetric version on the line, which is a different question. Asymmetric variants with unknown or random initial distance were treated later by others.
events.direction: Solves the asymmetric continuous-line variant. Different question from the symmetric discrete problem; recorded because the article covers continuous rendezvous.

events.what_happened: Donglei Du, Q. Han, Juan Vera and Luis F. Zuluaga, 'Improved bounds for the symmetric rendezvous search problem on the line', posted on Optimization Online in 2006 (May, per the URL path), published in Operations Research in 2008. Bounds the symmetric rendezvous value on the line at initial distance 2 to the interval (4.1520, 4.2574), improving the previous interval (3.9546, 4.3931), and conjectures the asymptotic value 4.25 from numerical calculations. The paper calls the problem 'a notorious open problem in the field of rendezvous search'.
events.revisions: Operations Research, May–June 2008 (journal version; abstract details not checked against it).
events.delivers: Bounds the symmetric rendezvous value on the continuous line at initial distance 2 to (4.1520, 4.2574). Gives no exact value.
events.remains: The exact symmetric value at initial distance 2 (conjectured 4.25) and the discrete problem. A different question from the discrete symmetric problem (continuous line), but in the family the article covers.

checked_by.who: Operations Research (refereed journal; referees not named)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for publication in 2008

events.direction: Moves the bound on a continuous symmetric value (interval narrowed); no exact value. Different question from the discrete problem.

events.what_happened: A. Ta-Shma and U. Zwick, 'Deterministic rendezvous, treasure hunts and strongly universal exploration sequences', SODA 2007. A deterministic algorithm for two agents with distinct labels on a graph, with time polynomial in the number of vertices and in the label. Not opened; the bound is as described in a secondary search summary (roughly n⁵ times the label, after activation of the second agent, with backtracking).
events.delivers: A deterministic rendezvous algorithm on general graphs with labelled agents. A different question from the symmetric discrete problem, but within the deterministic section of the article.
events.remains: Better deterministic bounds were later given by others; the deterministic variant is a separate open area.
events.direction: Deterministic variant, a separate question from the symmetric problem. No bearing on the discrete symmetric open case.

events.what_happened: Richard Weber, 'The optimal strategy for symmetric rendezvous search on K3', arXiv:0906.5447, 30 June 2009. Proves that the Anderson–Weber strategy is optimal for symmetric rendezvous on the complete graph with three vertices (n = 3), confirming the roughly 20-year-old conjecture. Published as 'Optimal Symmetric Rendezvous Search on Three Locations', Mathematics of Operations Research 37(1):111–122, 2012 (journal details from search snippets).
events.revisions: v1 30 June 2009 only on arXiv. Journal version Mathematics of Operations Research 37(1), 2012, pp. 111–122 (search snippet; not opened).
events.delivers: For n = 3 (K3): the Anderson–Weber strategy is optimal among symmetric strategies, with its value. Restricted to n = 3.
events.remains: n ≥ 4 (optimality of Anderson–Weber for n ≥ 4, the optimal value and the asymptotic constant).

checked_by.who: Mathematics of Operations Research (refereed journal; referees not named)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the n = 3 result

events.direction: Confirms the Anderson–Weber strategy is optimal for n = 3 (repairing the 1990 claim). Consistent with the question.

events.what_happened: Richard Weber, 'The Anderson–Weber strategy is not optimal for symmetric rendezvous search on K4', arXiv:0912.0670, submitted 3 December 2009 (v1; no later versions). Exhibits a symmetric strategy for n = 4 that does better than Anderson–Weber, 'by only a tiny fraction of a percent' (abstract, as summarised). No journal publication found. Cembrano, Fischer and Klimm (2026) describe this as an 'unpublished manuscript' that 'finally gave concrete evidence that an improvement is possible for n=4', and say its calculations 'are not made explicit but are feasible with the help of a computer'.
events.revisions: v1 only (3 December 2009); 6 pages per comments field.
events.delivers: For n = 4 only: a symmetric strategy with smaller expected meeting time than Anderson–Weber, by a very small margin. Whether the n = 4 improvement is established by an explicit argument, rather than by computation, is what I could not confirm: the PDF body was not readable through my tool and Cembrano et al. describe the calculations as not explicit.
events.remains: All n ≠ 4, the exact optimal value for n = 4, and the general question.
events.time_since_posted: About 16 years (since 3 Dec 2009); no journal publication found.
events.doubts: Cembrano, Fischer and Klimm (2026) call this 'concrete evidence' and say the calculations are 'not made explicit but are feasible with the help of a computer', which means the argument may not be a complete explicit proof. I could not read the paper's body to check. No journal publication or independent verification was found.
events.direction: Cuts against Anderson–Weber optimality for n = 4 (the question's own direction). Scope: n = 4 only.
events.object: A symmetric strategy for n = 4 that modifies Anderson–Weber over blocks of 12 steps (as described by Cembrano et al.) and has slightly smaller expected meeting time. The abstract does not give the strategy in closed form in the parts I read; the improvement is described as numerical in the later account.

events.what_happened: Varsha Dani, Thomas P. Hayes, Cristopher Moore and Alexander Russell, 'Codes, Lower Bounds, and Phase Transitions in the Symmetric Rendezvous Problem', arXiv:1609.01582, submitted 6 September 2016 (v1 only). Changes the objective to maximising the probability of meeting within T steps. For T ≈ 4n a symmetric strategy meets with probability 1−o(1), and no symmetric strategy with T = αn for α < 4 does so. Anderson–Weber is asymptotically optimal for T ≤ n, but not for large T. Gives a lower bound of 0.638n (Proposition 9, 0.6389n, stated not tight) on the expected meeting time of any symmetric strategy. Published in Random Structures & Algorithms, 2016 (venue from a search snippet; not opened).
events.delivers: A lower bound on the expected meeting time of symmetric strategies on the discrete problem: at least 0.638n asymptotically (not tight). Separately, results for the probability-within-T objective (phase transition at T ≈ 4n), a different question.
events.remains: The gap between the lower bound 0.638n and the Anderson–Weber upper bound 0.829n, and the exact asymptotic constant. The probability-within-T objective is a different question.

checked_by.who: Random Structures & Algorithms (refereed journal; venue from a search snippet)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record, if the venue is as reported
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper in 2016 (not verified by me)

events.direction: Moves a lower bound on the discrete symmetric expected-time quantity (0.638n), so it is a bound moving on the core problem; it also answers a changed objective (probability within T), which is a different question.

events.what_happened: Marthe Bonamy, Michał Pilipczuk and Jean-Sébastien Sereni, 'On the effect of symmetry requirement for rendezvous on the complete graph', arXiv:2002.03764, submitted 10 February 2020 (v1 only). Shows that for every n ≥ 2, if the two players must use the same strategy, the expected waiting time is at least (n+1)/2 + εn with ε = 2⁻³⁶, against the asymmetric optimum (n+1)/2. Published in Mathematics of Operations Research with DOI 10.1287/moor.2022.1288, pp. 942–953 (journal details from search summaries; the INFORMS page returned HTTP 403 when I tried to open it). Search summaries say Weber is an author of the MOR version.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 10 February 2020 only. Published in MOR (online 2022, issue 2023 per search summaries).
events.delivers: A lower bound for the discrete symmetric problem: expected waiting time at least (n+1)/2 + εn for all n ≥ 2, with ε = 2⁻³⁶ in the arXiv version. It shows symmetry carries a linear cost over the asymmetric optimum. Does not reach the Anderson–Weber upper bound.
events.remains: The gap between (n+1)/2 + εn and the Anderson–Weber upper bound 0.829n; the exact symmetric optimum and its asymptotic constant.

checked_by.who: Mathematics of Operations Research (refereed journal; referees not named)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper (the published version may differ from arXiv v1, see doubts)

events.doubts: The constant is in conflict across sources: the arXiv v1 abstract gives ε = 2⁻³⁶; a search summary of the published MOR version gives 1/3600 (via a key lemma using an Ahlswede–Katona result); another summary gives an unreadable value. The INFORMS page returned HTTP 403, so the published constant is unresolved.
events.direction: Moves a lower bound on the discrete symmetric problem, and shows symmetric and asymmetric values differ asymptotically. Does not settle the optimum.

events.what_happened: Braun and Wierman, a paper on symmetric rendezvous search on the cube, hosted by the FAU combinatorics group (math.fau.edu/combinatorics/braun49.pdf). Per search summaries, it calls the 'astronaut problem' a famous open problem in search games and rendezvous, studies a symmetric rendezvous problem on the cube, and gives upper bounds and a common lower bound for the cube value. I could read only the PDF metadata (created 2018-02-01, typeset in LaTeX), not the body, so the content is not verified.
events.delivers: Unverified. According to search summaries, upper and lower bounds for symmetric rendezvous on a cube graph. A specific graph, a different question from the general discrete problem.
events.remains: Unverified; the cube value is not settled according to the summary.
events.doubts: Unverified: I could not read the body, and the cube result is known only from a search summary.
events.direction: Unverified. Likely a bound on a cube variant, not the general discrete problem.

events.what_happened: Drew Henrichsen (Johns Hopkins PhD candidate), talk 'Rendezvous Search on a Sphere: The Astronaut Problem', NIST ACMD Seminar, 6 February 2024. Two agents on a sphere (a featureless planet) with detection radius r and bounded speed. The abstract states the problem is decades old with no published results, and reports theoretical upper bounds that vary inversely with r, in both symmetric and asymmetric settings, plus Monte Carlo estimates. The speaker's bio says he has published a paper on rendezvous search on a sphere, but no title or venue is given. One search summary says it appeared in Naval Research Logistics vol. 72 no. 7 (30 April 2025); a second search found no such NRL paper, so that claim is unconfirmed.
events.revisions: No written argument found. Possible 2025 NRL paper, unconfirmed.
events.delivers: Upper bounds, inversely in the detection radius r, on the optimal meeting time for the continuous sphere (astronaut) variant, symmetric and asymmetric. No constants in the abstract.
events.remains: Exact values and the sphere problem in general. This is a different question from the discrete symmetric problem: a continuous variant with a detection radius, in the family the article covers.
events.time_since_posted: About 32 months since the talk; no written argument found.
events.doubts: No written argument, paper or venue was found for the bounds. The speaker's 2025 NRL paper is unconfirmed (one search summary reported it, a second did not find it).
events.direction: Upper bounds on a continuous variant (sphere, astronaut problem). Different question from the discrete symmetric problem.

events.what_happened: Yann Bourreau, Ananth Narayanan and Alexandre Nolin, 'Optimal Deterministic Rendezvous in Labeled Lines', arXiv:2505.04564, submitted 7 May 2025 (v1), revised 13 January 2026 (v2), stated to appear at STACS 2026. Two agents on an infinite line with unique integer labels, no communication, unknown initial distance D. Gives a deterministic algorithm running in O(D log* ℓ) with ℓ the largest label (refined to O(D log* ℓ_min)), improving Miller and Pelc's O(D² (log* ℓ)³) for unknown D and matching Miller and Pelc's lower bound Ω(D log* ℓ_max).
events.delivers: For deterministic rendezvous on the labelled infinite line with unknown initial distance: tight time O(D log* ℓ). Restricted to the labelled line.
events.remains: The labelled graph case in general, and the unlabelled symmetric problem (which this paper does not address, because labels break symmetry).

checked_by.qualification: Refereed conference; the arXiv comment says 'to appear'
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for STACS 2026 (acceptance inferred from 'to appear'; not independently confirmed)

events.direction: Settles the tight deterministic complexity on the labelled line for unknown distance. Different question from the symmetric discrete problem (labels break the symmetry); sits in the deterministic variant that the article covers.

events.what_happened: Javier Cembrano (Universidad de Chile), Felix Fischer (Queen Mary University of London) and Max Klimm (TU Berlin), 'Faster Symmetric Rendezvous on Four or More Locations', arXiv:2604.02058, v1 submitted 2 April 2026, v2 2 August 2026 (v2 content changes not identified). Constructs for every finite n ≥ 4 an explicit symmetric strategy ('First-Same-or-Different', FSD), a modification of Anderson–Weber in which consecutive tours of the non-home locations are correlated (the first elements of permutations in every third moving round, per a secondary summary). Its expected meeting time is strictly smaller than Anderson–Weber's. Exact improvement for n = 4 and a lower bound for n ≥ 5 are given in terms of the home-stay probability θ.
events.revisions: v1 2 April 2026; v2 2 August 2026. Content changes between versions not identified (the readable text of v2 was not compared with v1).
events.delivers: For every finite n ≥ 4, a symmetric strategy with strictly smaller expected meeting time than Anderson–Weber, so Anderson–Weber is not optimal for any n ≥ 4 (answering negatively the question open since 1990 of whether it stays optimal for larger n). For n = 4 an exact closed form for the improvement (transcribed from a fetch summary as 8(1−θ)⁶ / (81(8−(3θ²−2θ+1)³)), θ the home-stay probability); for n ≥ 5 the improvement is at least 483(1−θ)⁶/(n−1)⁸. Does not establish the optimal value for n ≥ 4 and does not identify an optimal strategy. Confirms the known n = 2 and n = 3 cases. The readable text gives no new upper bound on the asymptotic constant; the improvement lower bound decays like (n−1)⁻⁸.
events.remains: The optimal symmetric expected meeting time and optimal strategies for every n ≥ 4; the asymptotic constant (Anderson–Weber's about 0.829n remains the best known upper bound as far as I could determine); and Anderson–Weber's question whether the optimal expected time increases with n (reported open in the paper, per a secondary summary). The discrete problem's general question remains open.
events.time_since_posted: About 6 months (2 April 2026 to 13 October 2026); no journal, no commentary and no independent check found.
events.directly_checkable: The n = 4 closed-form improvement and the explicit FSD strategy can be checked by computing both expected meeting times for n = 4 at a given θ. I did not perform this check.
events.doubts: No journal record and no public check by anyone outside the authors. The acknowledgements, funding, AI-use statement, reference list and v2 change note were not readable (the arXiv HTML stopped at Appendix C.2 in both of my attempts; the PDF is not decodable through my tool). The n = 4 formula comes from a fetch summary of the HTML, not from the paper text I could read directly. The strategy's correctness has not been checked by anyone I could find.
events.direction: Cuts against the Anderson–Weber optimality question for every n ≥ 4: the strategy it names is strictly better than Anderson–Weber for each such n. Does not change the n = 2 and n = 3 results, and does not establish the optimal value for n ≥ 4.
events.object: An explicit symmetric strategy for each finite n ≥ 4 (FSD): Anderson–Weber modified by correlating consecutive tours of the non-home locations, guided by the clique structure of a graph on permutations (derangement structure). It is explicit and constructive (not a non-constructive existence proof), per the abstract ('we construct an explicit symmetric strategy'). For n = 4 its improvement over Anderson–Weber has the closed form above; for n ≥ 5 it is bounded below by 483(1−θ)⁶/(n−1)⁸. The authors' method is described as intuition and combinatorics of derangements, not computer search (per a secondary summary of the paper).

events.what_happened: Konstantinos Georgiou, Claude Gravel (a co-author; not a model), Joey Kapusin and Lazar Mandic, 'Oblivious Self-Distance Symmetric Rendezvous on the Integer Line', arXiv:2609.13632, v1 submitted 12 September 2026, v2 29 September 2026. Two agents at distance 2d on the integer line, symmetric, restricted to 'oblivious self-distance' strategies (each agent's decision depends only on its position relative to its own start). For the known-distance case: the exact value R_1 is determined and attained by a finite-support strategy; numerical bounds below 7.83d² for d = 2 to 6 (not proven globally optimal; the authors conjecture the weak-peek minimisers are global); R_d = Θ(d²) under the restriction; a universal strategy for unknown distance with O(d^(2+η)) expected time.
events.delivers: Within a restricted strategy class (oblivious self-distance), on the integer line: the exact known-distance value at d = 1, bounds for d = 2 to 6, and asymptotic Θ(d²). Does not address the unrestricted symmetric line problem, nor the discrete symmetric problem.
events.remains: Unrestricted symmetric line values for d ≥ 2 (the paper's bounds are restricted-class bounds), global optimality of the numerical minimisers, and the discrete problem.
events.doubts: The d = 2 to 6 bounds rest on numerical optimisation (Python with NumPy and SciPy, L-BFGS-B); the authors say the computed weak-peek minimisers are not proven global. The acknowledgements say an AI tool was used for code generation and debugging (recorded under ai), so the provenance of that code is a point a later reader may want to check.
events.direction: Different question: a restricted-strategy variant on the line. Does not cut for or against the discrete symmetric problem's conjectures.

systems.name: ChatGPT
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors' acknowledgements: an 'auxiliary tool for exploratory discussion, code generation and debugging', and used for 'consistency checks of intermediate arguments'. Whether the code generation feeds into the numerical bounds that are a stated result is not clear from the text I could read.
systems.basis_quote: The authors used ChatGPT as an auxiliary tool for exploratory discussion, code generation and debugging, [...] for consistency checks of intermediate arguments. All mathematical claims, proofs, computational results, and final verification are the sole responsibility of the authors. (Quoted from a summariser's reading of the HTML, not checked against the raw text; the ellipsis joins two passages the summary gave separately.)

disputes.summary: Who first showed Anderson–Weber is not optimal for n = 4: Weber (arXiv:0912.0670, December 2009) gave a better n = 4 strategy by a small margin, and Cembrano, Fischer and Klimm (2026) give an explicit closed form for n = 4 and the first result for all n ≥ 4. Cembrano et al. describe Weber's calculations as not explicit. Both are preprints and neither is journal-published in the sources I found.

Anderson and Weber (1990) claimed the optimal strategy for n = 3, and that claim is wrong; a valid proof was given by Weber (arXiv:0906.5447, 2009; Mathematics of Operations Research, 2012). The date of the repaired proof varies by source: 2009 (arXiv), 2012 (Wikipedia and Cembrano et al.), and 2006 (Weber's Cambridge problem page). I took the arXiv date as the first public written argument.

Constant in the Bonamy–Pilipczuk–Sereni lower bound: ε = 2⁻³⁶ in the arXiv v1 abstract, and a secondary summary of the published Mathematics of Operations Research version gives 1/3600. The INFORMS page returned HTTP 403, so I could not resolve it.

Wording of Weber's open question. As summarised from his problem page, the question asks whether there is a symmetric strategy with expected meeting time less than n. The Anderson–Weber strategy already achieves about 0.829n, so that literal question is answered yes. Either the page is loosely worded or the intended question is the optimum or the Anderson–Weber optimality question. This needs a check against the page's verbatim text, which I could not obtain (the fetch was summarised).

summary: The bullet is the bare title 'Rendezvous problem', so the scope was taken from the linked Wikipedia article (whose lead describes the rendezvous search family and names the symmetric discrete problem, the Mozart Café problem, as very hard) and from Weber's problem page, which states the discrete symmetric problem as its open question. Under that scope the events on the core discrete problem are: Anderson and Weber (1990), which settles n = 2 and wrongly claims n = 3; Weber (arXiv 30 June 2009), which settles n = 3 and was published in MOR 2012; Weber (arXiv 3 December 2009), which shows Anderson–Weber is not optimal for n = 4 by a small margin, with calculations that Cembrano et al. describe as not explicit; Dani, Hayes, Moore and Russell (arXiv 6 September 2016), which gives a lower bound of 0.638n on the expected time and changes the objective for other results; and Bonamy, Pilipczuk and Sereni (arXiv 10 February 2020; MOR 2023), which gives a symmetric lower bound of (n+1)/2 + εn. The only in-window event on the core problem is Cembrano, Fischer and Klimm (arXiv:2604.02058, 2 April 2026; v2 2 August 2026), which constructs an explicit symmetric strategy beating Anderson–Weber for every n ≥ 4, so Anderson–Weber is not optimal for any n ≥ 4; it gives an exact n = 4 improvement and a lower bound for n ≥ 5 (readable only via fetch summaries). Six months on it has no journal record, no commentary and no independent check that I could find. It does not identify the optimal value or an optimal strategy for n ≥ 4, and as far as I could tell it does not change the 0.829n upper bound, whose asymptotic optimality remains open. Other in-window events are on variants and are labelled as different questions: a sphere (astronaut problem) talk on 6 February 2024 with bounds in the detection radius and no written argument found; a deterministic labelled-line result (Bourreau, Narayanan and Nolin, 7 May 2025, STACS 2026) giving tight complexity on the labelled line; and a restricted-strategy line model (Georgiou et al., 12 September 2026). On AI: no source on the core problem names an AI system in the text I could read. The Cembrano et al. acknowledgements and AI statement were not reachable, so their none_found is conditional. The one AI-named event is Georgiou et al., whose acknowledgements say ChatGPT was used as an auxiliary tool for code generation and debugging; that paper is a different question, and the contribution is recorded as stated. Close calls: whether the Cembrano result counts as a partial resolution of the bullet (it settles a yes/no question about Anderson–Weber for n ≥ 4, but not the optimum or the asymptotic constant), and whether the line and deterministic variants belong to 'the' rendezvous problem at all (the statement does not say).
competing_reading: A reader could take the Cembrano et al. result as a real resolution of an explicit part of the problem: a question open since 1990 (whether Anderson–Weber is optimal for larger n) is now answered negatively for every n ≥ 4, with an explicit construction and an exact n = 4 formula, which is more than a bound moving. Against that, the bullet's named problem is the general rendezvous problem, whose main unknowns (the optimal value for each n, the asymptotic constant, and the monotonicity question) are untouched, and the paper is an unrefereed preprint with no check in six months. A second reading treats the variant events (sphere, labelled line, restricted line) as part of the family, which would change the count of in-window events on the bullet's question even though none of them moves the discrete problem.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The Cembrano et al. acknowledgements, AI-use statement, reference list and the v1 to v2 change note, read from the PDF or a full-text source; this decides the AI field for the one in-window event on the core problem. (2) Journal publication or an independent verification of the FSD strategy and the n = 4 formula. (3) The verbatim text of Weber's open-problem page, to fix which question the bullet asks (the literal 'less than n' version is already answered by Anderson–Weber). (4) The published constant in the Bonamy et al. MOR paper (2⁻³⁶ or 1/3600). (5) Whether the authors' main claims change the asymptotic constant 0.829n, which would settle whether the asymptotic part of the problem has moved. (6) The text of the 2024 sphere talk's written argument, if one exists, and the NRL 2025 paper if confirmed.

event.what_happened: Javier Cembrano (Universidad de Chile), Felix Fischer (Queen Mary University of London) and Max Klimm (TU Berlin), 'Faster Symmetric Rendezvous on Four or More Locations', arXiv:2604.02058, v1 submitted 2 April 2026, v2 2 August 2026 (v2 content changes not identified). Constructs for every finite n ≥ 4 an explicit symmetric strategy ('First-Same-or-Different', FSD), a modification of Anderson–Weber in which consecutive tours of the non-home locations are correlated (the first elements of permutations in every third moving round, per a secondary summary). Its expected meeting time is strictly smaller than Anderson–Weber's. Exact improvement for n = 4 and a lower bound for n ≥ 5 are given in terms of the home-stay probability θ.
event.revisions: v1 2 April 2026; v2 2 August 2026. Content changes between versions not identified (the readable text of v2 was not compared with v1).
event.delivers: For every finite n ≥ 4, a symmetric strategy with strictly smaller expected meeting time than Anderson–Weber, so Anderson–Weber is not optimal for any n ≥ 4 (answering negatively the question open since 1990 of whether it stays optimal for larger n). For n = 4 an exact closed form for the improvement (transcribed from a fetch summary as 8(1−θ)⁶ / (81(8−(3θ²−2θ+1)³)), θ the home-stay probability); for n ≥ 5 the improvement is at least 483(1−θ)⁶/(n−1)⁸. Does not establish the optimal value for n ≥ 4 and does not identify an optimal strategy. Confirms the known n = 2 and n = 3 cases. The readable text gives no new upper bound on the asymptotic constant; the improvement lower bound decays like (n−1)⁻⁸.
event.remains: The optimal symmetric expected meeting time and optimal strategies for every n ≥ 4; the asymptotic constant (Anderson–Weber's about 0.829n remains the best known upper bound as far as I could determine); and Anderson–Weber's question whether the optimal expected time increases with n (reported open in the paper, per a secondary summary). The discrete problem's general question remains open.
event.time_since_posted: About 6 months (2 April 2026 to 13 October 2026); no journal, no commentary and no independent check found.
event.directly_checkable: The n = 4 closed-form improvement and the explicit FSD strategy can be checked by computing both expected meeting times for n = 4 at a given θ. I did not perform this check.
event.doubts: No journal record and no public check by anyone outside the authors. The acknowledgements, funding, AI-use statement, reference list and v2 change note were not readable (the arXiv HTML stopped at Appendix C.2 in both of my attempts; the PDF is not decodable through my tool). The n = 4 formula comes from a fetch summary of the HTML, not from the paper text I could read directly. The strategy's correctness has not been checked by anyone I could find.
event.direction: Cuts against the Anderson–Weber optimality question for every n ≥ 4: the strategy it names is strictly better than Anderson–Weber for each such n. Does not change the n = 2 and n = 3 results, and does not establish the optimal value for n ≥ 4.
event.object: An explicit symmetric strategy for each finite n ≥ 4 (FSD): Anderson–Weber modified by correlating consecutive tours of the non-home locations, guided by the clique structure of a graph on permutations (derangement structure). It is explicit and constructive (not a non-constructive existence proof), per the abstract ('we construct an explicit symmetric strategy'). For n = 4 its improvement over Anderson–Weber has the closed form above; for n ≥ 5 it is bounded below by 483(1−θ)⁶/(n−1)⁸. The authors' method is described as intuition and combinatorics of derangements, not computer search (per a secondary summary of the paper).

events.credibility_reason: Later authors describe its calculations as not made explicit; never published or independently checked.
Talk only; no written argument found and the reported 2025 paper is unconfirmed.

judgement.why: The statement is a bare title; following the record, the core question is the discrete symmetric problem (optimal expected meeting time for each n). Line, sphere, cube, labelled-deterministic and restricted-strategy results are variants. The key close call is Cembrano–Fischer–Klimm: it answers negatively whether Anderson–Weber is optimal for n ≥ 4, but the statement names no such sub-question, and what the result does to the problem's quantity is lower the best-known upper bound on the optimal value for every n ≥ 4 while leaving the optimum open, so it is a bound (F4), not a case. The explicit FSD strategy is a record construction, not a counterexample to anything the statement asserts, so object_role is null. Pre-snapshot n = 2 (1990) and n = 3 (Weber 2009, MOR 2012) are journal-accepted cases; Weber's K4 note and the Dani et al. and Bonamy et al. lower bounds are bounds. Georgiou et al.'s ChatGPT use (exploratory discussion, code generation, debugging, consistency checks) credits it with no stated mathematics in the result, so none, and the event is a variant anyway.
judgement.doubts: Cembrano et al.'s AI statement and acknowledgements were unread, so its ai_role of none is conditional. Its n = 4 formula comes only from a fetch summary. If the bullet were read as asking specifically whether Anderson–Weber is optimal, Cembrano et al. would be a case (or whole for n ≥ 4) rather than a bound. Several journal acceptances (Alpern–Gal, Ta-Shma–Zwick, Dani et al.) are known only from snippets.
